questions.stem: The INDIAN PARLIAMENT is BICAMERAL, consisting of:

options.option_text: PRESIDENT + LOK SABHA (House of the People) + RAJYA SABHA (Council of States) — Art 79

questions.explanation: ARTICLE 79 — 'There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the PRESIDENT and TWO HOUSES to be known respectively as the Council of States (RAJYA SABHA) and the House of the People (LOK SABHA)'. So Indian Parliament has 3 components: (1) PRESIDENT — NOT a member of either House but integral to Parliament; bills need his assent; summons + prorogues both Houses; dissolves LS. (2) RAJYA SABHA (COUNCIL of STATES) — Upper House; MAX STRENGTH 250 (238 elected from states/UTs + 12 NOMINATED by President from fields of Literature, Science, Art, Social Service). Currently 245 seats (233 + 12). Permanent body, NOT SUBJECT TO DISSOLUTION; 1/3 members retire every 2 years → 6-year term. Indirect election by ELECTED members of STATE LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLIES (MLAs) via proportional representation by single transferable vote. Chairman = VICE-PRESIDENT of India (ex-officio). First sitting 13 May 1952. (3) LOK SABHA (HOUSE of the PEOPLE) — Lower House; MAX STRENGTH 552 (530 states + 20 UTs + 2 Anglo-Indians, but 2 Anglo-Indians removed by 104th CAA 2020); current 543 (with 2020 amendment — 2 Anglo-Indian seats lapsed). Members DIRECTLY elected from single-member constituencies (first-past-the-post); 5-year term (can be dissolved earlier). Age 25+. Speaker elected from among members. Quorum 1/10 of House (~55 for LS, ~25 for RS). PARLIAMENT SESSIONS: min 3 per year — (a) BUDGET (Feb-May); (b) MONSOON (Jul-Sep); (c) WINTER (Nov-Dec). MAX gap between sessions = 6 months (Art 85). New PARLIAMENT BUILDING inaugurated 28 May 2023 — triangular shape, designed by HCP (Bimal Patel of Gujarat). REFERENCES: President's address (Art 87, at start of every general election LS session + each year's first session), Question Hour, Zero Hour, Calling Attention, Adjournment Motions, No-Confidence Motion, Ordinance-making power (Art 123).

questions.stem: The MAXIMUM gap between two sessions of Parliament cannot exceed:

options.option_text: 6 MONTHS — Article 85(1); at least 3 sessions every year; President summons each house

questions.explanation: ARTICLE 85(1) — 'The President shall from time to time summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, but SIX MONTHS shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session.' PRACTICAL RESULT: at least 3 sessions every year. 3 REGULAR sessions: (1) BUDGET SESSION (Feb-May) — longest; Presidential address (joint sitting at start); Budget presentation; 2 PARTS — Part 1 (Budget presentation + general discussion), then 3-4 week gap for Standing Committees to scrutinise, Part 2 (voting on demands for grants + passing Finance Bill + Appropriation Bill). (2) MONSOON SESSION (Jul-Aug). (3) WINTER SESSION (Nov-Dec). GENERAL PROVISIONS: (a) SUMMONED by President (on advice of CoM); (b) PROROGUED by President (ends a session); (c) DISSOLUTION applies only to LS (Art 85(2)(b)); RS NOT dissolved (permanent body). (d) JOINT SITTING (Art 108) called by President when houses disagree on a Bill (except Money Bills + Constitutional Amendments). Only 3 joint sittings in Indian history — (1) 1961 Dowry Prohibition Bill; (2) 1978 Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill; (3) 2002 POTA (Prevention of Terrorism Act). Speaker presides. (e) Sessions can extend beyond 6 months with Presidential + Speaker's approval. (f) PARLIAMENT'S SITTINGS: LOK SABHA ~60-80 days/year recent, historically ~130+; RS ~50-70 days. Declining sitting days a concern. QUORUM: 1/10 of total strength each House (Art 100). ZERO HOUR: first hour after Question Hour (12 noon in LS), MP raises issue without notice; flexible. QUESTION HOUR: first hour (11 AM-12 noon). LAME DUCK session — last session of an outgoing LS after general election; members who lost election still attend (rare). No MP CAN be absent for 60 consecutive days without permission or seat vacates (Art 101).

questions.stem: A MONEY BILL (Article 110) can be introduced:

options.option_text: ONLY in the LOK SABHA, on PRESIDENT's recommendation; RAJYA SABHA can only RECOMMEND changes within 14 days (not binding)
By Finance Minister in joint session

questions.explanation: MONEY BILL — specially defined in Art 110. DEFINITION (7 specific matters exclusively): (a) Imposition/abolition/remission/alteration/regulation of ANY TAX; (b) regulation of Union borrowing; (c) Consolidated Fund custody/appropriation/withdrawal; (d) declaration of any expenditure as charged on CFI; (e) appropriation of CFI moneys; (f) CF-linked audit/payment; (g) ANY matter incidental to (a)-(f). NOT incidental taxes/cesses for local or special purposes. PROCEDURE: (1) Introduced ONLY in LOK SABHA (not RS); (2) only on PRESIDENT's prior RECOMMENDATION; (3) after LS passage, sent to RS; (4) RS has only 14 DAYS to return with RECOMMENDATIONS; LS may ACCEPT or REJECT them — not binding; (5) Deemed passed by both Houses after 14 days; sent to President for assent; (6) PRESIDENT can either ASSENT or WITHHOLD — CANNOT RETURN (unlike ordinary Bill). RS HAS NO VETO over Money Bills — LS supreme. SPEAKER's CERTIFICATE: Speaker of LS DECIDES if a Bill is Money Bill; decision FINAL + NOT REVIEWABLE by any court (per Art 110(3)). HOWEVER, SC has in recent cases (Roger Matthew, 2019; Aadhaar Puttaswamy-II 2018 — split view) said Speaker's decision IS subject to judicial review if it's manifestly wrong. FINANCE BILL (broader) vs MONEY BILL: (a) ALL Money Bills are Finance Bills, NOT vice versa. (b) Finance Bills Category A (Art 117(1)) — involve any Art 110 matter; require Presidential recommendation; only in LS. Category B (Art 117(3)) — involve expenditure from CFI; can be in either House but need Presidential recommendation. Ordinary Finance Bill (non-110 matters) — RS has full powers. RECENT CONTROVERSIES: (1) AADHAAR ACT 2016 passed as Money Bill (bypassing RS where NDA lacked majority); challenged — SC upheld in Puttaswamy-II (2018) 4-1 with Chandrachud's dissenting that it was NOT a Money Bill (hence misuse of Art 110). (2) 2017 Finance Bill amended several non-financial laws (PMLA, Companies Act, Tribunals) as Money Bill — challenged in Roger Matthew case; SC referred to 7-judge bench (still pending). MONEY BILL mechanism is a KEY CENTRE of power-imbalance debate between LS + RS.
questions.subject: Polity

options.option_text: Is ELECTED by LS members FROM AMONG themselves at first meeting; presides over LS; has CASTING VOTE in case of tie; remains in office until new LS meets
Is nominated by the ruling party

questions.explanation: SPEAKER OF LOK SABHA — Art 93. ELECTED by LS members from among themselves at the FIRST MEETING of a new Lok Sabha, presided over by PRO TEM Speaker (senior-most MP nominated by President, administers oath to new MPs; first task = Speaker election). POWERS + FUNCTIONS: (1) PRESIDES over LS sittings; (2) INTERPRETS Rules of Procedure (rulings not subject to judicial review per Art 122 on internal Parliament matters — with narrow exceptions); (3) maintains ORDER + decorum (suspension of members); (4) decides WHO SPEAKS (order of precedence); (5) CERTIFICATION of MONEY BILLS (Art 110(3)) — final; (6) presides over JOINT SITTING of two Houses (Art 108); (7) ADMITS motions, questions, resolutions per rules; (8) DECIDES on POINT OF ORDER; (9) only CASTING VOTE when tie; no vote otherwise; (10) decides DISQUALIFICATION on grounds of defection (10th Schedule — since Kihoto Hollohan 1993, subject to judicial review). TENURE: until the NEXT LS meets + elects a new Speaker — so continues through general election, unlike other MPs (who cease with LS dissolution). Thus when LS is dissolved, Speaker continues until just before first sitting of next LS. CAN BE REMOVED by RESOLUTION passed by effective majority (> 50% of total then-existing LS members) per Art 94(c); 14-day notice. Has VOLUNTARILY RESIGNED in past (Balram Jakhar 1989, Somnath Chatterjee 2009 out of CPI(M) expulsion row). DEPUTY SPEAKER — Art 93; also elected by LS; usually by OPPOSITION (convention, not mandatory). Currently (as of 2024-25) NO Deputy Speaker — this post was VACANT throughout 17th LS (2019-24), controversially. NOTABLE SPEAKERS: (1) G.V. MAVALANKAR (1952-56) — 'Father of Lok Sabha'; set conventions. (2) BALRAM JAKHAR (1980-89) — longest tenure (nearly 2 full terms). (3) RABI RAY, Shivraj Patil, Manohar Joshi. (4) SOMNATH CHATTERJEE (2004-09) — commanded respect across spectrum. (5) MEIRA KUMAR (2009-14) — FIRST WOMAN Speaker; daughter of Jagjivan Ram. (6) SUMITRA MAHAJAN (2014-19) — second woman. (7) OM BIRLA (2019-2024, 2024- current) — first Speaker re-elected to post. RS PRESIDING: Chairman = VP (ex-officio); Deputy Chairman = elected member.

questions.stem: A NO-CONFIDENCE MOTION against the Council of Ministers can be moved:

options.option_text: ONLY in LOK SABHA, by any MP with 50-MP support, under Rule 198 — Govt resigns if motion PASSES by simple majority

questions.explanation: NO-CONFIDENCE MOTION — procedure under RULE 198 of Rules of Procedure + Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha. KEY FEATURES: (1) MOVED ONLY IN LOK SABHA (not Rajya Sabha) — because CoM is COLLECTIVELY RESPONSIBLE only to LS (Art 75(3)). (2) Any MP can give notice; SPEAKER admits if has support of AT LEAST 50 MEMBERS; discussion then scheduled. (3) 10 days notice + discussion scheduled by BAC (Business Advisory Committee). (4) No specific reasons required; just loss of confidence in CoM asserted. (5) If motion PASSES by SIMPLE MAJORITY of members PRESENT + voting, entire CoM must RESIGN. (6) PM has option of advising dissolution instead; but no CoM can continue without LS confidence. HISTORY: First NC motion was moved in Aug 1963 by Acharya J.B. Kripalani against Nehru (defeated). ~27+ NC motions moved so far (till 2024); only 3 SUCCEEDED leading to government fall: (1) 1979 — Morarji Desai resigned before vote; Charan Singh-led minority JP(S) govt briefly; (2) 1990 — V.P. Singh lost NC motion + resigned; (3) 1997 — Deve Gowda lost NC (Cong withdrew support); (4) 1999 — ATAL BIHARI VAJPAYEE's NDA-1 (1998-99) LOST by just 1 VOTE — 269 to 270 — due to absence of Saifuddin Soz (who broke party whip) + Odisha CM Giridhar Gamang (who was Odisha CM but still voted as MP). MOST FAMOUS VOTE. SUBSEQUENTLY defeated: (5) 2003 — Sonia Gandhi's NC against Vajpayee (defeated). (6) 2008 — UPA-I faced TRUST VOTE after Left withdrew support over Indo-US nuclear deal; UPA won 275-256 amid chaotic scenes + 'cash-for-votes' scandal (SP + JD(U) defectors helped). (7) 2018 — NDA-I v. Modi NC (lost 126-325). RELATED MOTIONS: (a) CONFIDENCE MOTION — moved by PM/Govt to prove majority; rare. (b) CUT MOTIONS — disapproval of government policy; rejects demand for grant (by symbolic ₹100, or actual amount, etc.); if passed = govt has to resign (treated like NC). (c) CENSURE MOTION — disapproval of specific policy / minister; does not require govt to resign. (d) ADJOURNMENT MOTION — brings LS business to halt to discuss urgent matter; needs 50 MPs; censure implicit. (e) PRIVILEGE MOTION.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The ANTI-DEFECTION LAW is in which SCHEDULE of the Constitution?

options.option_text: 10th SCHEDULE — added by 52nd CAA (1985); further amended by 91st CAA (2003) to remove 1/3 split exemption

questions.explanation: ANTI-DEFECTION LAW (Aaya Ram Gaya Ram Act) — added as 10th SCHEDULE to Constitution via 52nd CAA 1985 (Rajiv Gandhi era). Named after Haryana MLA GAYA LAL who changed parties 3 times in 1 day in 1967 — 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' phrase born. DISQUALIFICATION GROUNDS under 10th Schedule: (1) VOLUNTARILY GIVING UP membership of his ORIGINAL party; (2) VOTING OR ABSTAINING contrary to party WHIP (directive) WITHOUT prior permission — within 15 days; (3) If INDEPENDENT MEMBER joins a party after election; (4) If NOMINATED MEMBER joins a party after 6 months of taking seat. EXCEPTIONS (original 1985): (a) 'SPLIT' if 1/3 or more members broke off — protected (allowed new group formation without disqualification). (b) 'MERGER' if 2/3 of legislature party agreed to merge with another — not defection. 91st CAA 2003 REMOVED the 1/3 SPLIT exemption (misused for profiteering); now only MERGERS with 2/3 support protected. ADJUDICATION: presiding officer of House (Speaker in LS, Chairman in RS, Speaker in Assembly) decides on disqualification. KIHOTO HOLLOHAN v. ZACHILLHU (1992) — SC held Speaker's decision is JUDICIALLY REVIEWABLE. NOTABLE cases: (1) Rajendra Singh Rana v. Swami Prasad Maurya (2007). (2) Madhya Pradesh Assembly crisis 2020 — 22 Cong MLAs resigned, Speaker accepted; Kamal Nath govt fell; Chouhan took over. (3) Maharashtra 2022 — Shinde faction split Shiv Sena; delayed Speaker's ruling; SC Subhash Desai 2023 remanded. (4) Telangana + Karnataka defections in 2019-2024 — multiple disqualification cases. CRITIQUES: (1) party-centric democracy — diminishes MP's individual judgment; (2) Speaker bias — ruling party's choice often sympathetic; (3) DELAYS by Speaker = de facto impunity; (4) merger threshold 2/3 too low — horse-trading still happens (just wholesale instead of retail). RECOMMENDATIONS: (a) NCRWC 2002 — decide anti-defection cases within 3 months. (b) Goswami Committee, Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), Law Commission. (c) 2020 SC Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil case suggested TIME-BOUND decision (3 months). NO LEGAL TEETH yet added. STRENGTHENING the anti-defection law is a long-pending reform.

questions.stem: A constitutional AMENDMENT BILL under Article 368 requires:

options.option_text: SPECIAL MAJORITY — majority of TOTAL membership + 2/3 of members PRESENT + VOTING in EACH House; some amendments additionally need ratification by 1/2 of states

questions.explanation: ARTICLE 368 — power of Parliament to AMEND the Constitution. 3 TYPES of amendments: (1) SIMPLE MAJORITY (not under Art 368 technically, but common) — for certain matters NOT covered by Art 368: e.g., admission/creation of new states, alteration of state boundaries (Art 2-4), citizenship provisions (Art 5-11 of Part II but NOT FRs), abolition/creation of Legislative Councils (Art 169), salaries of judges, etc. Only simple majority in both Houses. (2) SPECIAL MAJORITY — required for MOST constitutional amendments under Art 368 (including FRs, DPSPs, basic framework). Requires: (a) majority of TOTAL membership of each House (>50% of house's total strength, not just present); (b) 2/3 of MEMBERS PRESENT + VOTING in each House. Both conditions must be satisfied in each House. NO joint sitting available for constitutional amendments. (3) SPECIAL MAJORITY + STATE RATIFICATION — required for 'federal provisions' that affect Centre-State balance. Same special majority + RATIFICATION by at least HALF the state legislatures (not 2/3 states — that's a common misconception). Matters requiring state ratification: (a) Art 54 + Art 55 — Election of President; (b) Art 73 + 162 — extent of executive power of Union + States; (c) SC + HC provisions (Art 124-147, 214-231); (d) Art 245-255 — legislative relations; (e) Art 368 itself; (f) representation of states in Parliament; (g) any item in Union List/State List/Concurrent List of 7th Schedule. IN Total ~106 CAAs passed so far (as of 2024). STATES' RATIFICATION recent — 101st CAA (GST 2016) required state ratification; done. IMPORTANT CAAs: (1) 1st (1951) — 9th Schedule introduced for land reforms. (2) 24th (1971) — Parliament's power to amend FRs (overturned Golaknath). (3) 42nd ('mini-Constitution' Mar 1976) — most sweeping; 59 changes; curbed judicial review; FDs added; Socialist + Secular + Integrity added to Preamble; extended LS term 5→6 yrs; DPSP primacy over FRs (struck down by Minerva Mills 1980). (4) 44th (1978, Janata) — reversed many 42nd changes; LS term back to 5 yrs; abolished property right as FR. (5) 52nd (1985) — 10th Schedule anti-defection. (6) 61st (1989) — voting age 21→18. (7) 73rd + 74th (1992) — Panchayati Raj + ULG. (8) 86th (2002) — Art 21A, RTE. (9) 91st (2003) — CoM cap 15%. (10) 101st (2016) — GST. (11) 102nd (2018) — NCBC constitutional. (12) 103rd (2019) — EWS reservation 10%. (13) 105th (2021) — states' identify OBC. (14) 106th (2023) — Women's Reservation in LS + Assemblies (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, post-delimitation implementation).

questions.stem: The FIRST HOUR of every Parliament sitting is reserved for:

options.option_text: QUESTION HOUR (11 AM-12 noon) — Members ask questions to Ministers for oral (Starred) or written (Unstarred) answers; also Short-Notice Questions

questions.explanation: QUESTION HOUR — FIRST HOUR of every Parliamentary sitting (11:00 AM – 12:00 NOON). Key feature of parliamentary accountability — MPs can ask questions to Ministers. 3 TYPES of Questions: (1) STARRED QUESTIONS — oral answer sought, identified by ASTERISK (*); 20 permitted per day in LS; Minister answers orally; SUPPLEMENTARY questions allowed. (2) UNSTARRED QUESTIONS — written answer; up to 230 per day LS; no supplementaries. (3) SHORT NOTICE QUESTIONS — urgent matter of public importance; less than 10 days notice; ORAL answer; Speaker's permission. ROSTER: each day's Qs directed to specific ministries (fixed rotation — Monday = certain ministries, Tuesday = others, etc.). Notice period: 15 DAYS ordinary; 10 for short notice. MINISTER FREEDOM: can decline to answer if national security, judicial proceedings sub-judice, or too onerous (answer). PARLIAMENTARY STANDING COMMITTEE for each Q — Railways, Transport, Health, Defence, Finance etc. ZERO HOUR (12 NOON-1 PM) — INFORMAL; unique to Indian parliamentary practice (NOT mentioned in Rules, started 1962). MPs raise urgent issues WITHOUT notice; flexible; Minister may or may not respond. Chaotic sometimes. Speaker's discretion to permit. OTHER KEY TIMES: (1) LUNCH BREAK (1-2 PM). (2) AFTERNOON SESSION (2-6 PM) — Bills, motions, discussions. (3) PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS: FRIDAY afternoons (2:30-6 PM) — Private Member's Bills + Resolutions. In practice, barely any Private Member Bill has passed (only 14 in Indian history; last in 1970). DEVICES to raise issues: (a) Calling Attention; (b) Adjournment Motion; (c) No-day-yet-named motion; (d) Short Duration Discussion (Rule 193); (e) Half-hour discussion; (f) Rule 377 mention. LOK SABHA daily business order: (1) Oath by new MP / VP (if any); (2) Obituary references; (3) Question Hour (11-12); (4) Zero Hour (~12-1); (5) Lunch; (6) Legislative business (Bills, discussions); (7) Resolutions. STANDING COMMITTEES: Parliament forms ~24 Department-Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) + Financial Committees (PAC, Estimates, Public Undertakings) + Department Committees (Business Advisory, Rules, Privileges, Govt Assurances etc.) — scrutinise Bills + budgets + reports.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE (PAC), which examines CAG reports, is:

options.option_text: A 22-member joint LS+RS committee; BY CONVENTION, chaired by a SENIOR OPPOSITION MP; scrutinises CAG audit reports of Govt expenditure

questions.explanation: PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE (PAC) — FINANCIAL COMMITTEE of Indian Parliament; examines CAG's reports on GOVT expenditure + audit. Est. 1921 (under Govt of India Act 1919). FORMATION: 22 MEMBERS (15 from Lok Sabha + 7 from Rajya Sabha); elected by Parliament ANNUALLY by proportional representation (single transferable vote) ensuring all parties + independents proportional representation. CHAIRMAN: appointed by SPEAKER of LS; by CONVENTION (not legal requirement) = a SENIOR MP from OPPOSITION party. This convention: (a) intended by M.N. Kaul, first Secretary-General of LS; (b) since 1967 regularly followed; (c) strengthens oversight — opposition MP chairs ≠ rubber-stamp. FUNCTIONS: (1) EXAMINE CAG REPORTS (audit on Consolidated Fund, Contingency, Public Account; appropriation accounts; finance accounts; audit of PSUs). Reports post-audit deviations, misappropriations, improper expenditure, systemic issues. (2) Scrutinise actual expenditure vs GRANTS passed by Parliament; flag excess, diversion, 'irregularities, losses, fraudulent' transactions. (3) Ensures ACCOUNTABILITY of executive for public money. (4) Reports SUBMITTED to Parliament annually (PAC typically produces ~20 reports each year). LIMITATIONS: (a) POST-FACTO examination only; (b) no direct power to punish; (c) recommendations TABLED; govt can reject (though rare); (d) scrutinises CAG reports only — cannot initiate suo-moto inquiries. FAMOUS PAC DISCOVERIES / cases: (1) BOFORS scandal (1987, chaired by V.K. Krishna Menon; reports controversial); (2) 2G SPECTRUM report (2011, chaired by Murli Manohar Joshi, BJP); (3) Coalgate, Commonwealth Games. RECENT CHAIRS: (a) BJP's Murli Manohar Joshi (2009-14 UPA-II); (b) Cong's K.V. Thomas, Mallikarjun Kharge (2014-19 NDA); (c) Cong's Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury (2019-24); (d) K.C. Venugopal (2024-). OTHER FINANCIAL COMMITTEES: (1) ESTIMATES COMMITTEE — 30 LS members; examines BUDGET ESTIMATES + efficiency; chaired by ruling party MP. (2) COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC UNDERTAKINGS (COPU) — 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS); examines CPSE performance + reports. DEPARTMENTAL STANDING COMMITTEES are SEPARATE (introduced 1993); examine ministry-wise demands for grants + Bills.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The WOMEN'S RESERVATION ACT (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), 2023 reserves:

options.option_text: 33% of seats (1/3) in LOK SABHA + STATE LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLIES for WOMEN — 106th CAA 2023; effective post DELIMITATION + census

questions.explanation: 106TH CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT ACT, 2023 / NARI SHAKTI VANDAN ADHINIYAM ('Women's Empowerment Law') — landmark legislation reserving 33% (1/3) of seats for WOMEN in LOK SABHA + STATE LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLIES + Delhi LA. PASSAGE: passed Sept 2023 during the SPECIAL SESSION (new Parliament building inauguration), in both LS + RS with near-unanimity. Signed by President Droupadi Murmu 28 Sep 2023. HISTORY OF DEMAND: (1) First Private Member Bill introduced 1996; failed several times thereafter — RS passed 2010 but never in LS. (2) 81st CAA Bill (2008), re-introduced as 108th CAA Bill (2010) — passed RS, lapsed in LS. (3) Finally in 2023 (17th LS) passed as 128th CAB → 106th CAA. KEY FEATURES: (1) 1/3 seats in LS + State Assemblies + Delhi LA. (2) RESERVATION ROTATION — constituencies reserved for women to ROTATE every election/delimitation. (3) HORIZONTAL RESERVATION — 1/3 of SC + ST seats also reserved for women from those groups. (4) ANGLO-INDIAN SEATS (now abolished) were excluded from scope. (5) DURATION — 15 YEARS initially; can be extended. IMPORTANT CAVEAT — EFFECTIVE DATE: will come into effect only AFTER: (a) NEXT CENSUS (delayed — due since 2021, now tentatively 2026 or later); (b) DELIMITATION EXERCISE based on census (freezing of seats currently freezes to 2026 population; after that, redistribution). So EARLIEST effective implementation: 2029 General Election (if 2026 census + delimitation done); 2034 realistic per some analysts. CURRENT WOMEN REPRESENTATION: LOK SABHA 2024: 74 out of 543 (~13.6%). RAJYA SABHA: 33/245 (~13%). STATE ASSEMBLIES: varies, range 7% (MP) to 16%. GLOBAL comparison: Rwanda (61%), Cuba (53%), Nicaragua (51%), Mexico (50%); UK ~35%, USA ~28%, India well below world average (~27%). PANCHAYAT + ULG — 1/3 reservation for women at local bodies since 73rd+74th CAAs (1992); many states have raised to 50% (Bihar first in 2006; now 21 states). CRITICISMS: (a) delay in implementation; (b) no OBC sub-quota (SC/ST included but not OBCs); (c) rotation creates 'temporary' constituencies, weakens long-term incumbents' service.
